question:
Identify the error in the given sentence and select the correct sentence from the given options.
This is the story of eight round planets, the few rocks in between, and some comets.
option_1: This is story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
option_2: This is a story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
option_3: This is the story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
option_4: This is the story of eight round planets, a few rocks in between, and some comets.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. This is the story of eight round planets, a few rocks in between, and some comets.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence incorrectly uses "the few rocks"; the correct expression is "a few rocks", since the sentence is making a general, indefinite reference to "some rocks", not a specific, already-identified set of rocks.

• Rule — "a few" vs "the few": "A few" is used before a plural countable noun to mean "some, a small number of" (a positive/indefinite sense). "The few" is used only when referring to a specific, previously mentioned or contextually definite small number of things (an exhaustive, "only these" sense).
◦ Example: I have a few friends in this city (some friends). / The few friends I have are very loyal (those specific, limited friends).

• Here, the sentence is simply describing the solar system in general terms — "the story of eight round planets, [some/a few] rocks in between, and some comets" — so the indefinite "a few" is required, not the definite "the few".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it drops the definite article before "story" — "This is story of..." should be "This is the story of...", since "the story of eight round planets..." refers to one specific, well-known account (the solar system).

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes "the story" to "a story"; since only one definite account of the solar system is being referred to, the definite article "the" is required, not the indefinite "a".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it retains the original error "few rocks" without the required article "a" before it — it should read "a few rocks".

NOTE

• Similarly confused pairs frequently tested by SSC: "little" vs "a little" (little = hardly any, negative sense; a little = some, positive sense) and "few" vs "a few" work the same way.

• Always check whether the reference is to a specific, already-known quantity (use "the") or a general, unspecified one (use "a/an" or no article).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Everyone have/ to join health orientation/ classes before/ going for trekking.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Everyone have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "Everyone have" contains the grammatical error; the correct form is "Everyone has".

• Rule — Indefinite pronouns as singular subjects: Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, no one, nobody are always treated as singular, and therefore take a singular verb (has/is/was, and third-person singular verb forms).
◦ Example: Everyone has to submit the form by Friday. (not "have")

• Applying the rule: since "Everyone" is singular, the verb must be "has", not "have" — so "Everyone have" is the erroneous segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to join health orientation" is grammatically correct — the infinitive "to join" correctly follows the modal sense of obligation set up by "has to".

• Option 3: "going for trekking" is grammatically correct — the gerund "going" is correctly used after the preposition "before".

• Option 4: "classes before" is grammatically correct as part of the phrase "classes before going for trekking" — there is no error of tense, agreement, or preposition here.

NOTE

• Other commonly tested singular indefinite pronouns: each, either, neither — these too always take a singular verb, e.g. "Each of the students has submitted the assignment."

• Do not confuse "everyone" (person, singular, one word) with "every one" (emphatic, two words, used with "of").

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Our plane / arrived at / the Mumbai airport / at the right time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. the Mumbai airport.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "the Mumbai airport" contains the grammatical error; the correct form is "Mumbai airport", without the article "the".

• Rule — Articles with proper-noun-based names: When a common noun (like airport, station, university, road) is preceded by a proper noun to form a specific, name-like compound (e.g., Mumbai Airport, Delhi Station, Oxford University), the compound behaves like a proper name and is generally NOT preceded by "the".
◦ Example: Our flight landed at Mumbai Airport. (not "the Mumbai Airport")

• Applying the rule: "the Mumbai airport" should simply be "Mumbai airport", since "Mumbai" already makes the airport's identity specific without needing the definite article.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "arrived at" is grammatically correct — the verb "arrived" is correctly followed by the preposition "at" to indicate the point of arrival.

• Option 2: "Our plane" is grammatically correct — the possessive adjective "Our" correctly modifies the singular subject "plane".

• Option 3: "at the right time" is grammatically correct — "the right time" correctly uses "the" since it refers to a specific, definite point in time (being on schedule).

NOTE

• Similar proper-noun compounds that usually drop "the": Mumbai Airport, Victoria Station, Connaught Place, Oxford University, Marine Drive.

• Contrast this with common nouns used generically, which DO take "the": e.g., "We reached the airport on time" (no specific name given, so "the" is used).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
It was noticed / that he truthful / answered the questions / raised by the Headmistress.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. that he truthful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "that he truthful" contains the grammatical error; the correct form is "that he truthfully".

• Rule — Adverbs modify verbs: A word that describes how an action is performed (i.e., modifies a verb) must be an adverb, not an adjective. Adjectives like "truthful" describe nouns/pronouns, while adverbs like "truthfully" describe verbs.
◦ Example: She truthfully answered every question. (not "truthful answered")

• Applying the rule: the word "truthful" is modifying the verb "answered" (describing how he answered), so it must take the adverbial form "truthfully", giving "that he truthfully answered the questions".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "It was noticed" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed passive construction introducing the noticed fact.

• Option 3: "raised by the Headmistress." is grammatically correct — the passive participle "raised" is correctly followed by the agent "by the Headmistress".

• Option 4: "answered the questions" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed verb-object phrase; the actual error lies in the adverb form preceding it, not in this segment itself.

NOTE

• Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding "-ly" to the adjective: truthful → truthfully, careful → carefully, quick → quickly.

• Watch out for adjective/adverb confusion pairs frequently tested by SSC: good/well, bad/badly, truthful/truthfully, honest/honestly, careful/carefully.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Our country, India, is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries of the world. With about 47,000 plant species, India (1)_____ tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia in plant diversity. There are (2)______ 15,000 flowering plants in India, which account for 6 per cent of the world's (3)_____ number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants, (4)_____ as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately 90,000 (5)____ of animals, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. occupies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill blank number 1 is "occupies" — "India occupies tenth place in the world..." meaning India holds/ranks in the tenth position.

• Rule — Subject-verb agreement in Simple Present Tense: With a singular subject (here, "India"), the main verb in the Simple Present Tense must take the third-person singular "-s/-es" form.
◦ Example: India occupies a significant place in Asia's plant diversity.

• Applying the rule: since the passage is a general, factual statement in the present tense and the subject "India" is singular, the verb must be "occupies".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "have" is incorrect because it is a plural-subject verb form; the singular subject "India" requires "has", and even "has" would not fit the intended meaning of "ranking/holding a position" as well as "occupies" does.

• Option 3: "had" is incorrect because it is the past tense form, but the passage is written throughout in the present tense to state general facts.

• Option 4: "occupy" is incorrect because it is the base/plural form of the verb; the singular subject "India" requires the third-person singular form "occupies", not "occupy".

NOTE

• "Occupy a position/place/rank" is a common collocation tested in cloze passages: e.g., "India occupies the fifth position in the world in terms of GDP."

• Always check the tense of the surrounding sentences in a cloze passage — a shift in tense form (present vs past) is a common way wrong options are created.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Our country, India, is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries of the world. With about 47,000 plant species, India (1)_____ tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia in plant diversity. There are (2)______ 15,000 flowering plants in India, which account for 6 per cent of the world's (3)_____ number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants, (4)_____ as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately 90,000 (5)____ of animals, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill blank number 2 is "about" — "There are about 15,000 flowering plants in India", meaning approximately 15,000.

• Rule — "about" as an approximation marker: "About" is used before a number to indicate an approximate quantity (roughly, nearly). It correctly fits before a large round figure like "15,000".
◦ Example: There are about 500 students in this school.

• Applying the rule: since the passage is giving an approximate count of flowering plants, "about" is the only word that grammatically and logically fits before the number "15,000".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a" is incorrect because the indefinite article "a" cannot be used before a plural countable noun phrase like "15,000 flowering plants".

• Option 2: "many" is incorrect because "many" is a quantifier used with a plural noun on its own (e.g., "many flowering plants"), not immediately before a specific number like "15,000".

• Option 3: "of" is incorrect because a preposition like "of" cannot grammatically precede a number in this position; it does not connect meaningfully with "15,000 flowering plants" here.

NOTE

• Common approximation words tested by SSC in cloze passages: about, around, approximately, roughly, nearly — all used before a number to indicate it is not exact.

• Do not confuse "nearly" (slightly less than) with "about"/"approximately" (close to, either more or less) in precise usage, though in most SSC cloze contexts they are treated as near-synonyms.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Our country, India, is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries of the world. With about 47,000 plant species, India (1)_____ tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia in plant diversity. There are (2)______ 15,000 flowering plants in India, which account for 6 per cent of the world's (3)_____ number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants, (4)_____ as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately 90,000 (5)____ of animals, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. total.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill blank number 3 is "total" — "which account for 6 per cent of the world's total number of flowering plants", meaning the overall/entire number.

• Rule — Word choice with "number of": When referring to the overall/complete count of something, the adjective "total" is used before "number of" to mean the grand/aggregate figure.
◦ Example: The total number of employees in the company is 5,000.

• Applying the rule: the passage is comparing India's flowering plants to the entire, overall count of flowering plants worldwide, so "total number" is the correct, natural collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "exact" is incorrect because "exact number" would mean a precisely known figure, which does not fit the sense of "the world's [total] number of flowering plants" here — the passage is speaking of the overall count, not precision.

• Option 2: "nearly" is incorrect because "nearly" is an adverb of approximation and cannot grammatically modify the noun phrase "number of flowering plants" in this position (it would need to precede a number, not "number of").

• Option 3: "exactly" is incorrect for the same reason as "exact" — it suggests precision, and also does not collocate naturally with "number of" here.

NOTE

• "Total number of" is a very common, natural collocation in formal/statistical writing, frequently tested in SSC cloze passages.

• Distinguish adjectives (exact, total) that modify nouns from adverbs (exactly, nearly) that modify verbs/adjectives/other adverbs — a common trap in cloze questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Our country, India, is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries of the world. With about 47,000 plant species, India (1)_____ tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia in plant diversity. There are (2)______ 15,000 flowering plants in India, which account for 6 per cent of the world's (3)_____ number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants, (4)_____ as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately 90,000 (5)____ of animals, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. such.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill blank number 4 is "such" — "The country has many non-flowering plants, such as ferns, algae and fungi", introducing examples.

• Rule — "such as" to introduce examples: The fixed phrase "such as" is used to introduce specific examples of a general category just mentioned.
◦ Example: She enjoys outdoor activities such as hiking, cycling and swimming.

• Applying the rule: "ferns, algae and fungi" are specific examples of the general category "non-flowering plants", so the correct connector is "such as".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "as" is incorrect because "as" alone (without "such") does not correctly introduce a list of examples in this context; it would need to be paired with "such" to form "such as".

• Option 3: "in" is incorrect because the preposition "in" does not fit grammatically or logically before a list of examples here.

• Option 4: "for" is incorrect because "for" does not function as an example-introducing connector; it does not fit the intended meaning of listing types of non-flowering plants.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "such as" (introduces examples) with "like" (can also introduce examples informally) and "for example / for instance" (used as a separate phrase, often after a comma).

• "Such as" is never followed by "etc." in formal writing, since "such as" already implies a non-exhaustive list.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Our country, India, is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries of the world. With about 47,000 plant species, India (1)_____ tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia in plant diversity. There are (2)______ 15,000 flowering plants in India, which account for 6 per cent of the world's (3)_____ number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants, (4)_____ as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately 90,000 (5)____ of animals, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. species.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill blank number 5 is "species" — "India also has approximately 90,000 species of animals", referring to the different kinds/types of animals.

• Rule — "species" is invariable: The word "species" has the same form in singular and plural (one species, many species); it is the standard scientific/biological term for a distinct kind of organism.
◦ Example: Scientists have identified over a million species of insects.

• Applying the rule: since the passage refers to a large count ("90,000") of distinct kinds of animals in a biological/scientific context, "species" is the correct and natural term, matching the earlier reference to "plant species" in the same passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "specie" is incorrect — "specie" is not the singular of "species"; it is in fact an unrelated word meaning "money in the form of coins".

• Option 3: "kind" is incorrect because, while not grammatically wrong in isolation, it does not match the precise, scientific register used earlier in the passage ("plant species"), and "90,000 kind of animals" would also need to be "kinds" to agree in number.

• Option 4: "type" is incorrect for the same reason as "kind" — it is less precise than "species" in this biological/statistical context and would need to be "types" to agree grammatically with "90,000".

NOTE

• Common invariable (same singular and plural) nouns tested by SSC: species, series, deer, sheep, aircraft, fish (fish can also take "fishes" for multiple species).

• "Specie" (singular, uncountable) vs "species" (singular or plural, countable) is a classic SSC vocabulary trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
She finished her quickly breakfast and rushed to school.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. finished her breakfast quickly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "finished her quickly breakfast" is grammatically wrong because the adverb "quickly" is wrongly placed between the possessive adjective "her" and the noun "breakfast".

• Rule — Position of adverbs of manner: An adverb of manner (like "quickly") should not split a possessive adjective + noun phrase (like "her breakfast"); it is normally placed after the object of the verb, at the end of the clause.
◦ Example: He completed his homework quickly. (not "his quickly homework")

• Applying the rule: the correct order is verb + object + adverb, giving "finished her breakfast quickly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "quickly her breakfast finished" is incorrect because it disrupts the normal Subject-Verb-Object word order entirely, placing the adverb before the verb-object phrase in an unnatural way.

• Option 3: "her breakfast finished quickly" is incorrect because it omits the main verb "finished" in its correct position relative to the subject "She", making "finished" read as a separate participial phrase rather than the main verb of the sentence.

• Option 4: "finished breakfast hers quickly" is incorrect because it wrongly uses the possessive pronoun "hers" (used without a following noun) instead of the possessive adjective "her" (used before a noun like "breakfast").

NOTE

• Adverbs of manner (quickly, slowly, carefully, quietly) are usually placed after the verb and its object, not between an article/possessive and its noun.

• Contrast with possessive adjectives (my, her, his, their) which must always be followed directly by a noun, unlike possessive pronouns (mine, hers, his, theirs) which stand alone.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
Lewis was aggressive, ________ (normal), moody, and brilliantly clever.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. eccentric.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed word is "normal", meaning usual, conventional, or conforming to a standard. (सामान्य)

• Its most appropriate antonym here is "eccentric", meaning unconventional or odd in behaviour or appearance; deviating from the usual or expected. (सनकी/असामान्य)
◦ Example: The eccentric professor wore mismatched socks to every lecture.

• Applying this to the sentence: "Lewis was aggressive, eccentric, moody, and brilliantly clever" — describing Lewis as unusual/unconventional fits naturally alongside the other unusual personality traits listed (aggressive, moody, brilliantly clever).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "feeble" (कमज़ोर): means weak or lacking strength — this is an antonym of "strong", not of "normal".

• Option 3: "dogmatic" (हठधर्मी): means asserting opinions as undeniably true without allowing debate — this is unrelated to "normal" and is not its antonym.

• Option 4: "selfish" (स्वार्थी): means concerned excessively with one's own interests — this is an antonym of "generous/unselfish", not of "normal".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "eccentric" often tested: quirky, odd, peculiar, unconventional, bizarre.

• Antonyms of "normal" also include: abnormal, unusual, strange, atypical.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I am scared of snakes; likewise, you are ________ of lizards.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fearful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses "likewise", a word that signals the second clause should express a similar/parallel feeling to the first clause.

• Rule — Parallelism with "likewise": "Likewise" means "in the same way / similarly", so the word used after it must match the sense of the earlier described feeling, here "scared".
◦ Example: I dislike loud noises; likewise, my sister is bothered by them too.

• Applying the rule: since the first clause says "I am scared of snakes", the parallel word must also express fear — "fearful" (afraid, scared) correctly matches this sense: "you are fearful of lizards".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "passionate" is incorrect because it means having strong enthusiasm or liking for something, which contradicts the parallel sense of fear required by "likewise".

• Option 2: "critical" is incorrect because it means expressing disapproval or being of crucial importance — neither meaning fits the required sense of fear.

• Option 3: "fond" is incorrect because it means having a liking or affection for something, which is the opposite of the fear expressed in the first clause.

NOTE

• "Likewise" and "similarly" are used to draw a parallel/similar point; contrast this with words like "however" or "on the contrary", which are used to signal an opposite or contrasting point.

• Words expressing fear often tested by SSC: fearful, afraid, terrified, apprehensive, frightened, petrified.

question:
Select the option that can substitute the bracketed word segment meaningfully.
Writing can instil a number of emotions (as in a reader).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. within a reader.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed segment "as in a reader" does not fit meaningfully with the verb "instil"; the correct preposition to use with "instil" is "within/in", in the sense of implanting or establishing a feeling inside a person.

• Rule — Collocation with "instil": The verb "instil" (to gradually establish an idea, feeling or attitude in a person's mind) is typically followed by "in" or "within" + person, meaning "inside" that person.
◦ Example: Good teachers instil confidence within their students.

• Applying the rule: "Writing can instil a number of emotions within a reader" correctly conveys that the emotions are being implanted inside the reader's mind.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "until a reader" is incorrect because "until" is a preposition/conjunction of time, which is meaningless when combined with "a reader" in this context.

• Option 2: "among a reader" is incorrect because "among" is used with three or more entities/a group, not with a single "a reader".

• Option 4: "instead a reader" is incorrect because "instead" must be followed by "of" (i.e., "instead of a reader") to function as a preposition; "instead a reader" is not a grammatically valid phrase.

NOTE

• "Instil" is commonly followed by "in/into/within" + person: instil discipline in children, instil fear into someone, instil confidence within a team.

• Do not confuse "among" (used for 3+ things/people) with "between" (used for exactly 2).

question:
Select the sentence which gives the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A piece of cake
option_1: Despite the heavy rain, they managed to have a successful outdoor event.
option_2: The restaurant was crowded, but they found a table without any difficulty.
option_3: The puzzle was so challenging that it took hours for Sam to solve it.
option_4: After months of practice, Emily performed her piano piece flawlessly during the concert.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The restaurant was crowded, but they found a table without any difficulty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A piece of cake" means something that is very easy to do or achieve, requiring little or no effort. (बहुत आसान काम)
◦ Example: The exam was a piece of cake for her since she had studied thoroughly.

• In Option 2, finding a table "without any difficulty" despite the crowd directly conveys the sense of an easy accomplishment, matching the idiom's meaning perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Despite the heavy rain, they managed to have a successful outdoor event" suggests overcoming a difficulty through effort, not something effortlessly easy — this does not match "a piece of cake".

• Option 3: "The puzzle was so challenging that it took hours for Sam to solve it" describes something difficult, which is the opposite of the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: "After months of practice, Emily performed her piano piece flawlessly" describes success achieved only after significant effort/practice, not something inherently easy — this does not match the idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "very easy", often confused with "a piece of cake": "child's play", "a walk in the park", "as easy as ABC/pie".

• Contrast with idioms meaning "very difficult": "a tough nut to crack", "an uphill task", "easier said than done".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Attire
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dress.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Attire" means clothing, especially fine or formal clothes worn on a particular occasion. (पोशाक/वेशभूषा)
◦ Example: Guests were requested to arrive in formal attire for the wedding reception.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Dress", which also means clothing/garments worn by a person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Park" (उद्यान): an open public area for recreation — unrelated in meaning to "attire".

• Option 3: "Theatre" (रंगमंच/थिएटर): a building or activity related to performing plays/drama — unrelated to clothing.

• Option 4: "Hotel" (होटल): an establishment providing lodging — unrelated to clothing.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "attire" often tested: apparel, garb, garments, clothing, costume.

• "Attire" can also be used as a verb meaning "to dress (someone) in fine clothes", e.g., "She was attired in a bright red saree."

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The dog was agitated and bit the child.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. serene.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "agitated" means troubled, anxious, or disturbed, especially so as to be visibly upset or restless. (व्याकुल/बेचैन)

• Its most appropriate antonym among the options is "serene", meaning calm, peaceful, and untroubled. (शांत)
◦ Example: Despite the chaos around her, she remained serene throughout the crisis.

• Applying this: a dog that is calm and untroubled (serene) is the direct opposite of a dog that is agitated (restless/upset), which fits the required antonym relationship.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "steady" (स्थिर): means firm, stable, or not shaking — closer to physical stability than to emotional calmness, and not the best antonym of "agitated".

• Option 2: "nerveless" (निर्भीक/शक्तिहीन): means either lacking courage/strength, or (in another sense) calm under pressure — an ambiguous and less precise fit compared to "serene".

• Option 3: "quiescent" (निष्क्रिय): means being in a state of inactivity or dormancy — this describes a lack of activity/motion rather than the emotional calmness that best opposes "agitated".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "agitated" often tested: anxious, disturbed, restless, upset, flustered.

• Other synonyms of "serene" often tested: calm, tranquil, placid, composed, peaceful.

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
He was thrilled when he heard about there journey to wonderland.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. there.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "there" is used incorrectly in the sentence; the correct word should be "their", the possessive adjective meaning "belonging to them".

• Rule — there / their / they're: "There" refers to a place or is used to introduce existence (there is/are); "their" is a possessive adjective showing ownership; "they're" is the contraction of "they are".
◦ Example: They kept their books over there before they're ready to leave.

• Applying the rule: "he heard about their journey to wonderland" requires the possessive "their" (whose journey — theirs), not the place-word "there".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "journey" is correctly spelt as used in the sentence.

• Option 2: "thrilled" is correctly spelt as used in the sentence.

• Option 4: "heard" is correctly spelt as used in the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone sets frequently tested by SSC: there/their/they're, to/too/two, its/it's, whose/who's, your/you're.

• A quick check: if "belonging to them" can be substituted, use "their"; if "are" can be substituted, use "they're"; otherwise, use "there".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I have observed that there is proper natural _____________ even at 6 o'clock on summer mornings.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. light.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word to fill the blank is "light", referring to natural daylight/brightness present at an early hour.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The blank must be filled with a word that collocates naturally with "natural" and fits the everyday, general register of the sentence describing morning brightness.
◦ Example: There was enough natural light in the room to read without switching on a lamp.

• Applying the rule: "proper natural light" is a natural, commonly used collocation describing the general brightness of daylight, which correctly fits the sentence about 6 o'clock summer mornings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "sparkle" is incorrect because it refers to small, bright flashes or glitter (as from a jewel or reflected light), not to general ambient daylight.

• Option 3: "lucent" is incorrect because it is an adjective (meaning shining/luminous), not a noun, and grammatically cannot be used as the noun following "natural" in this blank.

• Option 4: "gleam" is incorrect because it refers to a brief or faint flash/glow of light, not the steady, general natural brightness described in the sentence.

NOTE

• "Natural light" is the standard collocation used for daylight; "sparkle" and "gleam" describe momentary or reflected brightness, often of an object's surface.

• Remember to check the part of speech required by the blank — here a noun is needed, which immediately rules out the adjective "lucent".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Hypocrisy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Deceit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hypocrisy" means the practice of claiming to have moral standards or beliefs that one's own behaviour does not conform to; pretence and insincerity. (पाखंड/दिखावा)
◦ Example: His hypocrisy was evident when he preached honesty but lied to his own family.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Deceit", meaning the act of deliberately deceiving or misleading someone through pretence. (छल/धोखा)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Harm" (नुकसान): means damage or injury — unrelated to the idea of pretence.

• Option 2: "Sincerity" (ईमानदारी/निष्ठा): means genuineness and honesty — this is actually an antonym of "hypocrisy", not a synonym.

• Option 4: "Truth" (सत्य): means that which is factually correct — this is also opposite in sense to "hypocrisy", not a synonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "hypocrisy" often tested: pretence, insincerity, duplicity, sanctimoniousness.

• The related adjective is "hypocritical" and the noun for a person is "hypocrite".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Bliss
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Pleasure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bliss" means perfect happiness; great joy or contentment. (परम आनंद)
◦ Example: Spending the holiday with family in the hills was pure bliss for them.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Pleasure", meaning a feeling of happy satisfaction and enjoyment. (आनंद/खुशी)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Consecration" (अभिषेक/पवित्रीकरण): means the act of dedicating something formally to a sacred purpose — unrelated to happiness.

• Option 3: "Genesis" (उत्पत्ति): means the origin or beginning of something — unrelated to happiness.

• Option 4: "Avail" (लाभ उठाना/उपयोगिता): means to use or take advantage of an opportunity, or usefulness — unrelated to happiness.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "bliss" often tested: joy, ecstasy, euphoria, rapture, elation.

• "Bliss" is often used in the phrase "blissful ignorance", meaning happiness resulting from not knowing about a problem.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
I consider that every matter must be considered in every point of view.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. from every point.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "in every point" is grammatically incorrect in this context; the correct fixed expression is "from every point of view".

• Rule — Fixed prepositional phrase "point of view": The idiomatic expression meaning "perspective/angle of consideration" always takes the preposition "from" before "point of view" (e.g., from my point of view, from every point of view).
◦ Example: From every point of view, this decision seems beneficial for the company.

• Applying the rule: the sentence should read "every matter must be considered from every point of view", using "from" rather than "in".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "of every point" is incorrect because it does not form the correct fixed phrase; "of" cannot replace "from" before "every point of view".

• Option 3: "at every point" is incorrect because, while "at every point" is a valid phrase in other contexts (meaning "at each stage"), it does not correctly combine with the following "of view" to form the required idiomatic expression.

• Option 4: "on every point" is incorrect because "on" does not correctly precede "every point of view" as a fixed idiomatic phrase.

NOTE

• "Point of view" is always preceded by "from" when expressing a perspective: from my/your/his/every point of view.

• Do not confuse this with "on this point" (meaning "regarding this specific matter"), which uses a different preposition for a different meaning.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Condimnation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Condimnation" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "Condemnation", meaning the expression of strong disapproval, or the sentencing of someone to a punishment. (निंदा/दंडादेश)
◦ Example: The government issued a strong condemnation of the terrorist attack.

• Spelling key: CON + DEMN + ATION. Note the sequence "dem" followed by "n", giving "demn", not "dimn" as in the incorrect option. The word derives from the Latin "condemnare", meaning "to sentence/blame".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Intermingled" is correctly spelt — meaning mixed together thoroughly.

• Option 3: "Imprisonment" is correctly spelt — meaning the state of being confined in prison.

• Option 4: "Conglomerate" is correctly spelt — meaning a large corporation formed by merging several smaller firms, or a mass of varied things grouped together.

NOTE

• Related words with the same "-demn-" spelling pattern: condemn, condemnable, condemnatory.

• Other commonly misspelt SSC words with silent/tricky letters: government, environment, judgement/judgment, occurrence, embarrass.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The sun was shining bright and intense in the sky.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Strong.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "intense" means existing or occurring in an extreme degree; very strong or powerful. (तीव्र/प्रबल)
◦ Example: The intense heat of the afternoon sun made it hard to stay outdoors.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Strong", meaning having great power, force, or intensity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Mild" (हल्का): means gentle or not severe — this is actually an antonym of "intense", not a synonym.

• Option 3: "Subtle" (सूक्ष्म): means so delicate or precise as to be difficult to notice — this does not match the extreme, powerful sense of "intense".

• Option 4: "Weak" (कमज़ोर): means lacking strength or force — this is also an antonym of "intense".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "intense" often tested: fierce, extreme, powerful, acute, severe.

• Be careful not to confuse "intense" (extreme in degree) with "intensive" (thorough, concentrated effort), which is a related but distinct word often tested by SSC.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Under the weather
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To feel unwell.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Under the weather" means to feel slightly ill or unwell; not in one's usual good health. (थोड़ा अस्वस्थ महसूस करना)
◦ Example: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, so I might skip the gym.

• This idiom is believed to originate from sailors who, when feeling seasick, would go below deck to shelter from the bad weather — hence being "under the weather" came to mean feeling unwell.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To feel secure" does not match the idiom's meaning; it describes safety, not illness.

• Option 2: "To enjoy the weather" is a literal misinterpretation of the word "weather" in the idiom; the idiom is not literally about enjoying weather conditions.

• Option 4: "To work against the weather" is also a literal misreading of the idiom; the correct meaning has nothing to do with fighting weather conditions.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to health, often tested by SSC: "on the mend" (recovering from illness), "fit as a fiddle" (in very good health), "at death's door" (very seriously ill).

• Avoid interpreting idioms word-for-word; their meaning is figurative and must be learnt as a fixed expression.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Once bitten, thrice shy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. twice shy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct, standard form of this idiom is "Once bitten, twice shy", meaning a bad or painful experience makes a person cautious about repeating that experience. (एक बार धोखा खाने के बाद सतर्क हो जाना)
◦ Example: After losing money in that scheme, he never invested again — once bitten, twice shy.

• The given sentence wrongly uses "thrice shy" in place of the correct, fixed wording "twice shy"; idioms are fixed expressions and their wording cannot be altered.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "always shy" is incorrect because it changes the fixed wording of the idiom to a form that is not the standard, recognised expression.

• Option 2: "never shy" is incorrect because it reverses the intended meaning of caution into its opposite (fearlessness), which is not the idiom's sense.

• Option 3: "once shy" is incorrect because it does not match the standard fixed form of the idiom, which uses "twice", not "once", in the second half.

NOTE

• The idiom draws a parallel: "once bitten" (one bad experience) leads to "twice shy" (double the caution thereafter).

• Other idioms about caution/learning from experience often tested: "A burnt child dreads the fire", "Once burned, twice cautious", "Better safe than sorry."
